title: Few Words Before God
sum: Qohelet turns from what he has seen to what he advises. First he goes with his reader to the Temple (5:1–7). Watch how you walk there. Listening is better than a fool's sacrifice. God is in the heavens and you are on the earth, so let your words be few. If you vow something to God, pay it, and do not tell the Temple's messenger it was a mistake. Dreams, vapors and too many words go together; the answer to all of them is to fear God.

Then he looks at money (5:8–20). In the province the poor are oppressed while officials watch over officials. The lover of silver never has enough, the rich man cannot sleep, and a fortune can vanish in one bad deal, leaving a son with nothing; everyone leaves the world as naked as he came. Against this Qohelet sets what he has seen to be good and beautiful: to eat, drink and see good in one's toil through the days God gives. To be able to enjoy what one has is God's gift, and it keeps a person from brooding over how short life is.
readings: Read as advice on worship

5:1–7 is one of the few places where Qohelet speaks about religion directly. Read this way, the chapter teaches a reverent, honest faith: few words, kept promises, no bargaining with God, and a fear of God that keeps a person humble. It stands close to the prophets' warnings against empty sacrifice and to Jesus' warning against babbling in prayer.
Read as social criticism

5:8–17 sees a world of layered officials, squeezed peasants, anxious rich men and fortunes lost overnight. Read this way, the chapter is a clear-eyed report on the economy of a province under foreign rule, and a warning that money cannot buy security.
Read as the call to joy

5:18–20 is the second of Qohelet's great calls to enjoy life. Read this way, the whole chapter leads up to it: since wealth cannot be held and God cannot be managed, the wise course is to receive one's share of food, work and gladness as a gift.

views.H: The setting is the Second Temple and a Persian or early Greek province (medinah, 5:8), with tax-collecting officials stacked one above another, silver as money, and households that drew many mouths (5:11). Vows and offerings were part of ordinary Temple life (Deuteronomy 23:21–23; Psalm 66:13–14).
views.C: Critical scholars note that 5:1–7 uses the wording of Deuteronomy 23:21–23 and the language of the sacrificial laws (shegagah, 'unintentional sin'), so Qohelet knew the Torah. 5:9 is one of the most obscure verses in the book, and 5:17 is probably damaged: the Greek and 4QQoh-a do not have 'he eats'.
views.W: The theme that no one takes his goods with him at death (5:15) is shared by Egyptian harpers' songs, which also move from that thought to a call to enjoy the day. Qohelet differs in naming God as the giver of the share.
views.J: The rabbis used 5:1 to teach that prayers should be short (Berakhot 61a) and debated whether it is better not to vow at all (Nedarim 9a). The Targum turns the chapter toward the world to come: wealth without charity earns no reward there, and the 'messenger' is the angel of judgment.
views.X: Christians have heard 5:2 beside Matthew 6:7 and 5:10 beside 1 Timothy 6:10. Monks read the chapter as a call to leave wealth behind; Luther read 5:18–20 as praise of daily work and its fruits received with thanks from God.

deep.b: For Ecclesiastes 5–8 the Hebrew is the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), with its Ketiv and Qere readings. The Greek was read verse by verse in Rahlfs' critical edition for all four chapters, and in Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus for all of chapter 5 and for every verse of chapters 6–8 cited in a variant (Swete's verse numbers in chapter 7 run one ahead of Rahlfs'). The Dead Sea Scroll 4QQoh-a (4Q109), the oldest copy of the book, was read in the transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook for every verse it preserves in these chapters (English 5:14–18; 6:1, 3–8, 12; 7:1–10, 19–20). The Syriac Peshitta was read in the text of the Leiden edition for the verses where the witnesses differ. The Targum of Qohelet was read in Aramaic (the Rabbinic Bible text) and in Ginsburg's English for all four chapters. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ecclesiastes Rabbah and the Talmud passages cited were read in full. The Latin Vulgate was not consulted for this part.

A vow (neder) was a promise to God, usually made in trouble, to give him something if he answered: an offering, a gift to the sanctuary, a period as a Nazirite, even a child (Genesis 28:20–22; Numbers 6:2; 1 Samuel 1:11). The law did not require vows, but it required that a vow once made be kept (Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21–23), and it allowed some vows to be redeemed with money (Leviticus 27). The danger was the rash vow, made in a moment of fear or zeal and regretted later (Proverbs 20:25; Judges 11). Qohelet's advice draws all of this into a few lines: you are not obliged to vow, but if you do, pay promptly, and do not use the language of 'unintended sin' to get out of it.

Later Jewish teaching grew more cautious still. The Talmud records Rabbi Meir's view that it is best not to vow at all (Nedarim 9a), and the formula of annulment, Kol Nidre, came to be said before Yom Kippur. Jesus' teaching on oaths, "do not take oaths at all" (Matthew 5:34), is close to this caution. Christian churches later divided over vows to God, especially the lifelong vows of monks and nuns (see the card below).

5:8–9 is a sketch of empire seen from below. A medinah was a province of the Persian empire, and Judah was one (Nehemiah 1:3). Above the village headman stood tax farmers and local officials, above them the governor, above him the satrap of Beyond the River, and above all the Great King. Nehemiah says that the earlier governors "weighed the people down" (Nehemiah 5:15), and the people say they "borrowed silver on our fields and vineyards" to pay the king's tribute (Nehemiah 5:4). In the Greek period under the Ptolemies of Egypt, the system was even more layered. Qohelet's words "do not be shocked" do not excuse oppression; they describe a system in which each official answers only to the one above, and the poor at the bottom have no one to appeal to.

echoes: Deuteronomy 23:21–23; Numbers 30:2; Leviticus 4:2; 1 Samuel 15:22; Proverbs 20:25; Job 1:21; Psalm 49:16–17; Psalm 115:3; Matthew 6:7; Matthew 5:33–37; Luke 12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:6–10; 2:24; 3:13

settings.what: Advice on worship, prayer and vows
settings.by: Qohelet, now giving commands instead of reporting what he has seen
settings.to: a reader addressed as "you", a man able to go up to the Temple, offer sacrifices and make vows: the students and men of means for whom the book was written
settings.when: in the Second Temple period, when Jerusalem's Temple was the center of Judean worship
settings.why: To keep the wise from careless religion: rushing into God's presence, talking too much, making vows they will not keep and treating sacrifice as a way to manage God. Knowing that the hearers were educated and comfortable explains the target: not open sinners but the self-assured, who think they can handle God as they handle business.
settings.readers: Later Jewish readers drew from it rules for short prayer and caution with vows; Christian readers set it beside Jesus' teaching on prayer and oaths.

settings.what: Reflections on oppression, money, loss and God's gift
settings.to: the same readers, people who handled money, paid taxes and dealt with officials in a province under foreign rule
settings.when: in the Persian or early Greek period, as most scholars think
settings.why: To loosen the grip of wealth on those who have it. Officials exploit, money never satisfies, riches can vanish, and death takes everything; what remains is the share God gives day by day. The passage moves the reader from anxiety about getting and keeping to gratitude for what can be enjoyed now.
settings.readers: For readers in every age who work for a living and worry about money, the passage is a sober check and a permission to enjoy; Christian monks heard a call to give wealth up, and Reformers a call to receive it with thanks.
views: Choon-Leong Seow and others read the money language (silver, income, owners, bad ventures) against the new money economy of the Persian province of Yehud.
Others, such as Thomas Krüger, find the layered officials of 5:8 closer to the bureaucracy of Ptolemaic Egypt's rule over Judea in the 200s BC.

traditions.q: Is it good for Christians to make lifelong vows to God, such as the vows of monks and nuns?
views: Yes. A vow is "a deliberate and free promise made to God concerning a possible and better good" and is an act of devotion (Catechism 2102, quoting the Code of Canon Law, canon 1191). The vows of poverty, chastity and obedience in religious life are praised by the Church, and like every vow they must be kept (5:4).
Yes. Monastic vows, taken at tonsure, are an ancient path of repentance and prayer, and monks and nuns are honored in the Church. They are free, not required of anyone.

Vows that bind the conscience to earn grace are not binding. The Augsburg Confession (Article 27) teaches that monastic vows made to merit forgiveness, or that cannot be kept, conflict with the gospel, and that leaving such vows to marry is not sin.

Vows are a lawful act of worship when made to God alone, freely and about things lawful (Westminster Confession 22.5–6), but "monastical vows of perpetual single life, professed poverty, and regular obedience" are called "superstitious and sinful snares" (22.7).

title: Riches Without Rest
sum: Chapter 6 shows the other side of the gift described at the end of chapter 5. Some people have everything (riches, property, honor) and are not allowed to enjoy it; a stranger eats it instead (6:1–2). A man may have a hundred children and live for centuries, but if he never gets his fill of good and is not even buried, a stillborn child is better off, for at least it has rest (6:3–6). All human toil feeds the mouth, and the appetite is never filled (6:7–9).

The chapter ends the first half of the book with questions. What has been has already been named; humans cannot argue with one stronger than they are; more words only make more vapor. Who knows what is good for a person in his brief shadow of a life, and who can tell him what will come after him (6:10–12)? The second half of the book takes up those two questions.
readings: Read as a lament

Read this way, the chapter is one of the darkest in the Bible: a list of lives that have everything and still come to nothing, ending in the judgment that a stillborn child is better off. It gives words to people who find that success has not brought satisfaction.
Read as a hinge
Read for its structure, the chapter closes the first half of the book with its last 'chasing the wind' (6:9) and opens the second with the questions 'Who knows?' and 'Who can tell?' (6:12).
Read as a warning about desire

The key word is nefesh, the appetite. Read this way, the problem is not wealth itself but a craving self that is never filled, and the remedy is to enjoy 'what the eyes see' instead of what the appetite chases (6:9).

views.H: The rich man whose goods go to a foreigner (6:2) fits a province where land and wealth could pass to outsiders through debt, confiscation or the absence of an heir. Burial and a remembered name (6:3–4) were the marks of a good end.
views.C: Scholars since Addison Wright have seen 6:9–10 as the midpoint of the book, where one set of refrains gives way to another. Some think 6:10–12 is the introduction to the second half rather than the end of the first.
views.W: Egyptian laments such as the Dispute between a Man and his Ba welcome death as a release, and Greek writers said that it is best never to be born. Qohelet uses it to measure, not to praise, death: what makes a life worth living is the ability to enjoy good.
views.J: The Targum reads the chapter as a warning to the rich who do no good with their wealth: the stranger who eats it is the man who marries the widow of one who died childless, and the one place where all go is Gehenna for sinners.
views.X: Christians have read 6:7 beside Jesus' words that life is more than food (Matthew 6:25) and Augustine's prayer that the heart is restless until it rests in God (Confessions 1.1). 6:12, 'who knows what is good', has been heard as a question that only revelation can answer.

deep.h: The two halves of the book
deep.b: In 1968 Addison G. Wright proposed that Ecclesiastes has a careful structure hidden under its rambling surface. In the first half (1:12–6:9) the sections end with the refrain "vapor and chasing the wind" (1:14; 1:17; 2:11; 2:17; 2:26; 4:4; 4:6; 4:16; 6:9). In the second half (6:10–11:6) the sections end with "cannot find out" and "who knows?" (for example 7:14; 7:24; 8:7; 8:17; 10:14; 11:6). The questions of 6:12, "who knows what is good?" and "who will tell what comes after?", announce those two themes. Wright also counted 222 verses in the book and found its midpoint at 6:9–10. Not every scholar accepts his scheme, and many think the book is looser; but the shift he noticed is real: the first half asks whether toil brings gain, the second whether anyone can know.

Three times Qohelet says that the unborn or the dead are better off than the living: in 4:2–3, the one who never existed; here in 6:3–5, the stillborn; and in 7:1, the day of death. Job cursed his birth in the same way (Job 3), and so did Jeremiah (Jeremiah 20:14–18). These are not calls to suicide, which none of these books recommends. They are measurements: a life that has goods but no joy in them is worse than no life at all. Qohelet's positive answer comes in the passages that frame this one: to be able to eat and enjoy is God's gift (5:18–20), and "light is sweet" (11:7).

echoes: 5:18–20; 4:2–3; 3:20; 1:9; Job 3:11–16; Jeremiah 20:14–18; Deuteronomy 28:30–33; Proverbs 16:26; Proverbs 27:20; Psalm 144:4; Job 14:2; Matthew 6:25; Luke 12:15–21; James 4:14

settings.what: Reflections on wealth that cannot be enjoyed, and the limits of knowing
settings.to: the book's readers, people who had or hoped for wealth, family and long life, and assumed these would satisfy
settings.when: at the close of the first half of the book, after the call to enjoy God's gift in 5:18–20
settings.why: To show that the blessings everyone wants (riches, honor, many children, long life) do not by themselves give satisfaction, and that humans can neither argue with God nor know what is coming. It drives readers to receive enjoyment as God's gift rather than to expect it as the reward of success.
settings.readers: Jewish readers who heard the book at Sukkot, the harvest festival, heard this chapter as a check on the pride of plenty; Christian readers heard in 6:12 a question that only God can answer.

title: Better Than
sum: Chapter 7 opens with a string of 'better than' sayings in the style of Proverbs, many of them startling (7:1–14). A good name is better than good oil, the day of death than the day of birth, the house of mourning than the house of feasting, grief than laughter, a wise man's scolding than a fool's song. Patience is better than pride; nostalgia is unwise; wisdom shelters like money and gives life. God makes both the good day and the bad, so that no one can know what comes next.

Then Qohelet tests wisdom against life (7:15–29). He has seen the righteous perish and the wicked live long, so he warns against being too righteous or too wicked; no one on earth does good without sinning. He tried to become wise and wisdom stayed far away. He went looking for the sum of things and found a woman more bitter than death, one man in a thousand, and no woman. His final finding is broader: God made human beings upright, but they have gone looking for many schemes.
readings: Read as wisdom sayings

Read this way, 7:1–14 is a small anthology of proverbs, chosen or written to turn ordinary values upside down: sorrow teaches more than pleasure, and the end of a matter shows its worth. Qohelet speaks here like the teachers of Proverbs, though with a darker edge.
Read as a test of wisdom

Read this way, 7:15–29 is a report of an experiment that fails. The tidy rule of reward breaks down (7:15), wisdom stays out of reach (7:23–24), and the attempt to add up life ends in a confession that humans, not God, have made life crooked (7:29).
Read as dialogue

Many scholars think Qohelet quotes views in order to test them. Read this way, the hardest lines of the chapter, on being too righteous (7:16) and on the woman more bitter than death (7:26–28), are claims Qohelet holds up to the light, and 7:29 is his own verdict.

views.H: The house of mourning and the drinking feast (7:2), bribery (7:7), city councils of leading men (7:19) and household slaves (7:21) belong to the social world of Qohelet's well-off readers in Persian or Hellenistic Judea.
views.C: Critics discuss whether 7:1–14 is Qohelet's own or collected sayings, whether a line has dropped before 7:7, and whether the feminine verb in 7:27 hides 'says the Qohelet'. The frame narrator's 'says Qohelet' in 7:27 is one of the clues that the book is a report about Qohelet.
views.W: The praise of the day of death (7:1) has parallels in Greek writers such as Herodotus and Sophocles, and 'nothing in excess' was the Greek motto many readers hear behind 7:16–18. The style of 7:1–14 is that of Israel's own proverb collections.
views.J: The Talmud set 7:3 against 2:2 among the book's contradictions (Shabbat 30b) and read 7:16 as God's rebuke to Saul for sparing Agag (Yoma 22b). Rashi takes the woman of 7:26 as heresy; the Targum, as a bad wife; Ecclesiastes Rabbah, among other readings, sees Abraham and Sarah in 7:28.
views.X: Christians have heard 7:20 in Paul's 'no one righteous' (Romans 3:10) and read 7:29 as a summary of creation and the fall. Jerome and the monks prized 7:2–4 as a call to remember death; 7:16 has been used both against self-righteousness and, wrongly, as an excuse for moderate sin.

deep.b:
Few verses in the Bible sound as strange as 7:16. Read in context, it follows 7:15: the righteous man perishes in his righteousness, the wicked lives long. So Qohelet warns his reader not to be righteous "too much" and not to "act the wise man to excess", and in the next breath not to be wicked too much or a fool. Four main readings have been offered.

  • A golden mean. Avoid extremes of strictness and of sin. Readers often compare the Greek motto "nothing in excess" and Aristotle's teaching that virtue lies between two vices.
  • Against self-righteousness. R. N. Whybray argued that the Hebrew verbs mean to think oneself righteous and to pose as wise (the reflexive titchakkam, as in Exodus 1:10). The target is a piety that expects to be paid.
  • A rabbinic reading. The Talmud (Yoma 22b) hears the words as God's rebuke to Saul, who in his pity spared Agag and the best of Amalek's flocks (1 Samuel 15), and then slaughtered the priests of Nob without pity; Rashi and the Targum follow this line.
  • Worldly prudence. Some modern readers find a cynical shrug: neither saints nor great sinners do well, so keep out of trouble.

Whatever the reading, 7:18 names the way through: "the one who fears God will come through all of them", and 7:20 shows that the danger of being too righteous is the danger of thinking oneself righteous, since no one on earth does good without sinning.

deep.h: The woman more bitter than death (7:26–29)
deep.b:
These verses are among the hardest in the book for modern readers. Taken at face value, 7:26 calls "the woman" a deadly trap, and 7:28 says Qohelet found one man in a thousand but no woman. The Plain translates them as they stand. Readers have answered them in several ways.

  • A misogynist view. Many critics say plainly that the verses share the low view of women common in the ancient world, and that honest reading should admit it.
  • A particular woman. Many commentators note the article, "the woman", and the language of the seductress in Proverbs 5–7 (snares, nets, bitterness, the escape of the righteous). On this view Qohelet warns against a type, as Proverbs does, not against women; elsewhere he urges enjoying life "with the woman you love" (9:9).
  • A figure. The woman may be Folly personified, the counterpart of Lady Wisdom (Proverbs 9:13–18). Rashi took her as heresy; the Targum as a quarrelsome wife whom a righteous man divorces.
  • A quoted view, tested and rejected. Norbert Lohfink argued that 7:26 quotes a saying, perhaps a popular misogynist proverb, and that 7:27–29 dismantle it: Qohelet says he is "still seeking" and has "not found", and his one certain finding is that God made human beings, all of them, upright, and "they" have gone looking for schemes. On this reading the passage ends by putting men and women in the same place.

Ancient readers also noticed that the voice is Solomon's, a king with a thousand women (1 Kings 11:3), and that the frame narrator breaks in here ("says Qohelet", 7:27), perhaps to mark the words as Qohelet's report rather than the narrator's own judgment.

deep.title: Claude's theory: an audit that does not balance
deep.b: This is Claude's own reading, not a published one, though it builds on what Seow and others say about Qohelet's commercial vocabulary. 7:23–29 is written like an accountant's report. Qohelet sets out to find the cheshbon, the sum or balance (7:25); he works "adding one to one" (7:27), the way a clerk tallies items; he reports a ratio, "one in a thousand" (7:28). Then the books will not balance. The only entry he is sure of is that God made humankind straight, while humans keep chishshevonot, "sums" of their own (7:29). The joke, if it is one, is that the auditor discovers that the accounts were falsified by the people being audited, himself included. Read this way, the hard sayings of 7:26–28 are entries in a ledger that Qohelet himself says he could not close.

echoes: Proverbs 22:1; Proverbs 14:29; Proverbs 16:32; Proverbs 5:3–4; Proverbs 7:22–27; Proverbs 9:13–18; 1:15; 3:14; 1 Kings 8:46; 1 Kings 11:3; Psalm 143:2; Job 2:10; Isaiah 45:7; Genesis 1:27; Genesis 3; Romans 3:10–12; Romans 5:12

settings.by: Qohelet, speaking in the style of Israel's proverb collections
settings.to: students of the wise who knew Proverbs, and anyone tempted to judge life by pleasure, success and good times
settings.when: at the start of the second half of the book, after the questions of 6:12
settings.why: To answer 'who knows what is good?' (6:12) with a list of surprising goods: sorrow over laughter, rebuke over flattery, endings over beginnings, patience over pride. The sayings teach the young and the comfortable to face death and hard days honestly, and to accept that God makes both kinds of day.
settings.readers: These sayings were among the most quoted parts of the book in Jewish and Christian teaching on mourning, humility and patience.

settings.what: Advice on righteousness, wisdom and the curses of others
settings.to: readers trained to expect that the righteous prosper and the wicked perish
settings.why: To keep the reader from two errors: a strict righteousness that expects reward and is crushed when it fails, and a wickedness that rushes to an early death. Since no one is sinless (7:20), the wise should also be slow to take offense at what others say (7:21–22).
settings.readers: Later readers used 7:20 as proof that all have sinned; 7:16 was read in Judaism as a warning against misplaced mercy and in Christianity as a warning against self-righteousness.

settings.what: Qohelet's report of his search for wisdom and the sum of things
settings.by: Qohelet, with the frame narrator breaking in at 7:27 ("says Qohelet")
settings.to: the book's readers, presented with Solomon's voice and his famous wisdom
settings.when: in the middle of the second half, as Qohelet tests his own method
settings.why: To admit the limits of wisdom: what has been is deep beyond finding, and the attempt to add up life turns up only fragments. The passage ends with the one finding Qohelet is sure of, that God made humans upright and they invented schemes.
settings.readers: Jewish and Christian readers have argued over 7:26–28 for centuries; many have read 7:29 as a summary of Genesis 1–3.
views: Some readers take 7:26–28 as Qohelet's own low view of women.
Lohfink and others read 7:26–28 as a common saying that Qohelet tests and refutes with 7:29.
A warning against one kind of woman
Many commentators see the seductress of Proverbs 5–7, or Folly personified.

traditions.q: Can a believer, by God's grace, live in this life without sinning (7:20)?
views: No one can avoid all sins, even venial ones, through a whole life without a special privilege from God, as the Church holds of the Virgin Mary (Council of Trent, Decree on Justification, canon 23). Yet by grace the justified can keep God's commands and avoid mortal sin.

No. The believer is at once righteous and a sinner (simul iustus et peccator): righteous by faith in Christ, yet still sinning daily, so that the confession of 7:20 and 1 John 1:8 stays true until death.

No. Sanctification is real but "imperfect in this life"; there remain "some remnants of corruption in every part" (Westminster Confession 13.2). No one since the fall can keep God's commands perfectly in this life.

Yes, in a sense. John Wesley taught Christian perfection: a believer can be made perfect in love and freed from willful sin in this life, though not from mistakes and infirmities. He answered 7:20 and 1 Kings 8:46 by saying they describe life before the gospel, not what grace can do now (sermon 'Christian Perfection', 1741).

The goal of the Christian life is theosis, union with God, and the saints grow toward it; yet the Church prays daily for forgiveness, and no one but Christ is called sinless. The question is framed as growth, not as a state of sinlessness reached.

title: The King's Word and the Limits of Knowing
sum: Chapter 8 begins at court (8:1–9). The wise man can interpret a matter, and wisdom softens a hard face. Obey the king's word, mindful of the oath before God; do not storm out of his presence or dig in on a bad cause, for no one can ask the king 'What are you doing?' There is a time and a judgment for everything, but no one knows what is coming, no one is master of the wind or of the day of death, and there is no discharge from that war.

Then Qohelet faces justice delayed (8:10–17). He has seen the wicked buried with honor in the city where they did wrong; because sentence is slow, people's hearts are set on evil. He knows it will go well for those who fear God, yet he sees the righteous get what the wicked deserve and the reverse. So he praises joy: eat, drink and be glad, for that will stay with you through the days God gives. And he ends with a confession: however hard anyone searches, even the wise, no one can find out the work of God.
readings: Read as court advice

Read this way, 8:1–9 is practical counsel for officials who served absolute rulers: be wise, obedient, patient and careful, because the king's power is real. It sits beside Proverbs' sayings about kings and the stories of Joseph, Daniel and Esther.
Read as an argument about justice

Read this way, the chapter sets traditional faith (8:12–13) beside honest observation (8:10, 14) and refuses to give up either. Its answer is not a theory but a way of living: fear God, enjoy his gifts, and admit what cannot be known.
Read as a confession of limits

The chapter is full of what humans cannot do: question the king, know the future, hold back the wind, escape death, find out God's work. Read this way, it prepares for the call to seize the day in chapter 9.

views.H: The court advice fits the Persian or Hellenistic world, with its absolute kings, loyalty oaths sworn in the name of the gods, and conscription without exemptions (8:8). Pitgam, 'ruling', is a Persian loanword (8:11).
views.C: Scholars debate whether 8:12b–13 is Qohelet's own belief, a quotation of conventional teaching he then answers in 8:14, or a pious gloss by a later editor. 8:10 is textually difficult, and many follow the Greek's 'praised' for the Hebrew 'forgotten'.
views.W: Ancient Near Eastern courtier wisdom, from Egypt to the Aramaic Ahiqar, gives the same advice to watch one's step before the king. Qohelet adds that the king, too, is subject to death and to the time that no one controls.
views.J: Rashi reads 8:2 both of God, the King of the world, and of foreign kings, to be obeyed in taxes but not in idolatry, like the three young men in Daniel 3. The Targum answers 8:14 with the world to come, where the righteous receive their full reward.
views.X: Christians have read 8:2–4 beside Romans 13:1–7 and 1 Peter 2:13–17, with the limit of Acts 5:29. Luther's praise of 8:15 as the right use of God's gifts stands against monastic readings; 8:17 has been set beside Romans 11:33 as an admission that God's ways cannot be traced.

deep.b: 8:10–14 is Qohelet's fullest treatment of the failure of justice. He sees three things: the wicked honored in death (8:10), sentence against evil delayed, which encourages more evil (8:11), and the righteous and wicked receiving each other's deserts (8:14). Between them he sets a confession of faith: "I also know that it will be good for those who fear God" (8:12–13). Readers have handled the tension in four ways. Some, following Robert Gordis, think Qohelet quotes the accepted teaching in order to test it. Some critics, such as George Barton, assigned the pious lines to a later editor. Michael Fox argues that Qohelet holds both beliefs at once, and that this is the meaning of hevel here: the absurd gap between what must be true and what is seen. Jewish and Christian tradition, beginning with the Targum, answers with a judgment beyond death, an answer the epilogue hints at (12:14) but Qohelet himself does not give. What he gives instead is 8:15: praise of joy, received as God's gift through the days he allots.

Qohelet's advice to courtiers (8:2–5) is cautious rather than idealistic. Obey because of the oath, do not walk out in anger, do not persist in what the king dislikes, for "whatever he wants, he does". The same caution appears in Proverbs (Proverbs 16:14; 20:2; 24:21) and in the stories of Jews serving foreign kings: Joseph, Nehemiah, Esther and Daniel. Those stories also show the limit. When a king commanded idolatry, Daniel's friends refused (Daniel 3:16–18), and Rashi reads 8:2 with that limit built in. Christians have read Qohelet beside Paul's call to be subject to the governing authorities (Romans 13:1–7) and the apostles' answer that God must be obeyed rather than human beings (Acts 5:29).

echoes: Proverbs 16:14; Proverbs 20:2; Proverbs 24:21; Daniel 2:4; Daniel 3:16–18; Job 9:12; Deuteronomy 20:5–8; Esther 1:20; Job 21:7; Malachi 3:13–18; Psalm 73; Isaiah 22:13; Luke 12:16–21; Romans 13:1–7; Acts 5:29; Romans 11:33; 3:11; 3:17

settings.by: Qohelet, speaking as a sage (8:2, "I say")
settings.to: young men who served or hoped to serve at court, as scribes, officials or advisers to a powerful ruler
settings.when: under Persian or Hellenistic kings whose word no one could question, perhaps after an oath of loyalty
settings.why: To keep them alive and useful: obey, be patient, choose the time, and do not provoke a ruler who can do whatever he wants. Then Qohelet sets even the king within limits: no one rules the wind, the day of death or the future.
settings.readers: For later readers living under rulers of every kind, the passage became a text on obedience to government and its limits.
views: Most scholars read 8:1–5 as practical counsel for officials, like Proverbs' sayings on kings.
The Targum and Rashi also read 'the king' as God, whose commands are to be kept.

settings.what: Reflections on delayed justice, joy, and what cannot be known
settings.to: readers who believed that God rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked in this life
settings.when: after the court advice, as Qohelet turns from the king's judgments to God's
settings.why: To be honest about what readers could see in their own city, where the wicked were buried with honor and sentence was slow, without giving up the fear of God. The passage teaches them to live with the tension: fear God, enjoy his gifts, and admit that the work of God cannot be found out.
settings.readers: Jewish and Christian readers have answered these verses with the hope of judgment after death, and have often quoted 8:17 when God's ways seemed hidden.
